title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to generate a fake interview between a Reserve Bank governor and a media personality, falsely endorsing an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fabricated article was designed to deceive people into treating the platform as legitimate. This represents a deployment of AI for impersonation and fraud rather than any authorized application.

The failure is one of AI capability being applied without authorization to create convincing false content at scale. The scam worked because there was no human verification step between the fabrication and its circulation, and because the output mimicked trusted sources. It would have taken either preventing unauthorized access to the generative system, or introducing verification requirements for content that claims to depict real people in interviews they did not give.

It is not established whether a single AI model or platform was responsible, or how the fraudulent article was distributed to reach potential victims.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never occurred, but the fabricated story was designed to promote the platform as a legitimate investment opportunity. This scam represents a growing trend of AI-generated deception targeting Australians.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows investment scams using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians are becoming increasingly sophisticated. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, media personality Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated Australians. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing, warning that familiar branding and convincing testimonials do not guarantee legitimacy.
